title: Berlin to Oslo: the Dancer, the Doctor, and the Hardest No
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Berlin, a dancer is born
stops.campa: Elsa Lindenberg is born in Berlin in 1906, a daughter of the working city: the Berlin of tenement courtyards, factory whistles and Sunday allotments. The capital she enters is about to become the capital of the dancing body: within her childhood Berlin will fill with movement choirs, gymnastic reformers and barefoot prophets, and the canon of German dance will count her among its emigrant daughters. From the beginning the family has little money, and the child has one estate only: a body that listens.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Elsa Lindenberg, 1932, plates in Myron Sharaf's Fury on Earth
sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa_Lindenberg
https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q20752182

stops.name: Berlin, the Helene Lange school, the scholarship child
stops.campa: Thirteen years old, Elsa enters the Helene Lange school in Berlin as a scholarship pupil, and her dance training begins. It is 1919: the Kaiser is gone, the Republic is hungry, and the city's answer to hunger is movement: Ausdruckstanz, the expression-dance, is being invented street by street. A scholarship child among the daughters of the Bürgertum, she earns her place with her body. The training is disciplined and free of charge, and she will never afterwards dance for anyone who has not earned her yes.
suggested_refs: Berlin girls'-school photographs of the early Weimar years
sources: Lilian Karina & Marion Kant, Hitler's Dancers (2003)
https://spartacus-educational.com/Elsa_Lindenberg.htm
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich, https://www.courtenay-young.co.uk/courtenay/articles/Elsa_Lindenberg_and_Reich.pdf

stops.name: Halensee, the villa of Hertha Feist, the Laban school
stops.campa: In a villa in Halensee, Elsa enrolls in the school of Hertha Feist, Laban's apostle in Berlin: the school for body-culture and dance where movement choirs, gymnastics, sunlight and the master's swings and scales make a single doctrine of the body. Here she takes the Laban training entire: space-harmony, effort, the body as a crystal of directions. She completes her diploma in 1927. The lineage is exact: Laban to Feist to Elsa, the mountain of Monte Verità come down to a Berlin garden.
suggested_refs: Laban-Gruppe von Hertha Feist, Berlin, dance-study photographs, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin
sources: Lilian Karina & Marion Kant, Hitler's Dancers (2003)
https://www.deutsches-tanzarchiv.de/archiv/nachlaesse-sammlungen/f/hertha-feist
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Charlottenburg, the Städtische Oper, the corps de ballet
stops.campa: Diploma in hand, she is engaged as a group dancer in the ballet of the Städtische Oper on the Bismarckstraße, and for six seasons the scholarship girl dances in the great house of Charlottenburg. The corps is discipline made nightly flesh: swan maidens, temple dancers, the operatic underworld. In these same years Laban himself ascends to the Prussian State Theatres across town; the new dance and the old house negotiate nightly in her joints. By day she goes looking for other rooms and other teachers.
suggested_refs: The Städtische Oper (Deutsche Oper) building on Bismarckstraße, Berlin-Charlottenburg
sources: Lilian Karina & Marion Kant, Hitler's Dancers (2003)
https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa_Lindenberg
Frank Woods, Dancer in the Light: The Life of Gerda 'Pitt' Geddes (2008)

stops.name: Berlin, the quiet room of Elsa Gindler
stops.campa: In a quiet Berlin studio Elsa finds the other pole of her art: Elsa Gindler, who teaches almost nothing and changes everything: sitting, standing, breathing attended to until the body reorganizes itself from within. Gindler writes nothing down; the work passes hand to hand like a rite. Lindenberg becomes her student and remains one across the ruin of the century, before the war and after it. Between Laban's great spatial crystals and Gindler's microscopic attention, the dancer now holds both ends of the body's knowledge.
suggested_refs: Elsa Gindler, the single surviving essay 'Die Gymnastik des Berufsmenschen' (1926)
sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa_Lindenberg
Geuter, Heller & Weaver, 'Elsa Gindler and her influence on Wilhelm Reich', J. of Body, Movement & Dance in Psychotherapy 5:1 (2010)
David Boadella, Somatic Psychotherapy: its roots and traditions, Energy & Character 21:1 (1990)

stops.name: Wilmersdorf, the Künstlerkolonie, the Red Block
stops.campa: She lives among the writers and artists of the Künstlerkolonie at the Laubenheimer Platz in Wilmersdorf, and she is a Communist: a member of the Red Block cell of the colony, the red island Arthur Koestler will remember in The God That Failed. The dancers' Berlin and the workers' Berlin are one city in her. Nights of meetings, leaflets, watchfulness against the SA squads that raid the colony; days in the opera's rehearsal rooms. The Party knows her as dedicated and courageous; the police begin to know her too.
suggested_refs: The Künstlerkolonie Berlin at Laubenheimer Platz (today Ludwig-Barnay-Platz), Wilmersdorf
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth: A Biography of Wilhelm Reich (1983), p. 194
Arthur Koestler, in The God That Failed (1949)
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Berlin by night, the glue-pot and the posters
stops.campa: By night the dancer of the Städtische Oper walks the dark streets with a pot of glue and a roll of posters against Hitler, pasting the walls of Berlin with warnings. It is dangerous work, the SA also walks at night, and it is in this underground weather that the name of Wilhelm Reich first reaches her: the Party doctor who preaches that fascism is made in the body, in the strangled life of the masses. She has heard of him before she ever sees him.
stops.quote: I got to know Willie Reich when I used to walk around Berlin at night with a pot of glue and anti-Hitler posters.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Lindenberg, filmed recollection, quoted at Spartacus Educational, 'Elsa Lindenberg'
suggested_refs: Digne Meller Marcovicz, Wilhelm Reich, Viva Little Man (film, 2004), with interview footage of Elsa Lindenberg
sources: https://spartacus-educational.com/Elsa_Lindenberg.htm
Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 194

stops.name: Berlin, the May march, the meeting with Reich
stops.campa: On a Communist march in May, Elsa and Dr. Wilhelm Reich walk in the same column, and the attraction between them is immediate and admitted. He is the founder of Sex-Pol, analyst of the Berlin clinics, author of banned enlightenments; he is also married. They begin seeing each other regularly, and the affair is no secret. She is troubled by the falseness of the position and says so, for clarity is her nature. The canon marks this column of marchers as the meeting place of psychoanalysis and the dance.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Elsa Lindenberg taken in 1932, reproduced in Sharaf's Fury on Earth
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 194
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Berlin, the meeting with Annie Reich
stops.campa: Elsa will not live in a lie: she asks for and gets a face-to-face meeting with Annie Reich, wife of the man she loves. The two women sit opposite one another in the failing marriage's parlor and speak plainly. Annie, who has known other affairs and knows this one is different, essentially surrenders her hold, and afterwards writes to Elsa a single sentence: that Elsa's happiness will be built upon her tears. The sentence is kept, and the marriage dies through the winter.
suggested_refs: Gedenktafel for Wilhelm and Annie Reich, Berlin-Wilmersdorf
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 195
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Berlin, the night of the burning Reichstag
stops.campa: On the night of the twenty-seventh of February the Reichstag burns, and the Republic's ashes are used to bury the Republic. Reich, just returned from Denmark, sees the fire and understands; within days he is over the border. Elsa remains in the trap of Berlin: she has a contract, a family, a cell, a life. Between them now travel letters: he bombards her with pleas to come to Vienna, where his wife and children are; she refuses the triangle flatly. She will come to him free or not at all.
suggested_refs: Press photographs of the Reichstag fire, 27-28 February 1933
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 196
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Charlottenburg, cast out of the Opera
stops.campa: The new Reich reaches into the opera house: on the twenty-first of April Elsa Lindenberg is formally expelled from the ballet of the Städtische Oper under the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, charged with conduct damaging to the state. The state is correct: she has damaged it with glue and posters and will damage it more. With Ruth Abramowitsch and Ilse Larede she has stood against the brownshirts; now come the search of her apartment, the warrant, and the end of the Berlin stage.
suggested_refs: The Gesetz zur Wiederherstellung des Berufsbeamtentums of 7 April 1933, instrument of the purge
sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa_Lindenberg
Lilian Karina & Marion Kant, Hitler's Dancers (2003)

stops.name: Stettiner Bahnhof, the road north
stops.campa: In late May she chooses: not Vienna and the ménage, but Copenhagen and the man alone. From the Stettiner Bahnhof the trains run north to the ferries. She leaves the city of her whole life: school, villa, opera, colony, the walls she postered, carrying the two Berlins in her body, Laban's and Gindler's, the stage and the street. The Gestapo keeps her file open. Elsa Lindenberg goes into an exile that will last, with a few burning returns, the rest of her life.
suggested_refs: The Stettiner Bahnhof, Berlin's gate to the Baltic ferries, demolished 1962
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 196
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Copenhagen, the exile household
stops.campa: In Copenhagen the exiles make a household. Reich trains Danish students, among them Philipson and Leunbach, writes, and begins the descent from the word into the flesh: the work that will be called vegetotherapy is conceived in these rooms, and the canon is clear about its second parent. Elsa, trained by Laban and Gindler, is the somatic knowledge in the house; she begins studies of her own that will found her later art. Denmark watches the scandalous doctor, and the visa is a candle burning from both ends.
suggested_refs: First edition of Die Massenpsychologie des Faschismus (Verlag für Sexualpolitik, Copenhagen 1933)
sources: David Boadella, Wilhelm Reich: The Evolution of His Work (1973), p. 89
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Malmö, across the Sound
stops.campa: Denmark declines to renew the doctor's visa: psychiatrists complain, a newspaper savages, the Danish Party expels a man who never joined it. The household moves three miles across the Sound to Malmö. Exile becomes geometry: the Danish students ferry over on alternate days for their training, and Elsa ferries back, several days a week, to keep her dance work alive in Copenhagen. In the boarding-house between two hostile shores, the two of them keep a school of the future.
suggested_refs: The Copenhagen-Malmö ferry across the Øresund, lifeline of the 1933-34 exile
sources: David Boadella, Wilhelm Reich: The Evolution of His Work (1973), pp. 90, 111
Ilse Ollendorf Reich, Wilhelm Reich: A Personal Biography (1969), p. 26

stops.name: Berlin, Christmas among the endangered
stops.campa: At the turn of the year Elsa goes back into Germany, into the Reich itself, to see family and friends in Berlin, while Reich circles Europe testing London, Paris, Zurich and the Tyrol. The visit is quietly heroic: her name stands in police files, and the city she posters against now rules itself by warrant. In Berlin the lovers meet again in passing and travel north together to Malmö. She will keep returning to the city that wants her arrested, as if Berlin were a wound that must be personally inspected.
suggested_refs: Photograph of Reich and Elsa Lindenberg skiing, 1934, in Beyond Psychology
sources: Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich
David Boadella, Wilhelm Reich: The Evolution of His Work (1973), p. 111

stops.name: Malmö, the watched boarding-house
stops.campa: Malmö is a big village and the village is watching: a secret-service agent is set on the boarding-house where Reich and Elsa live, students are intercepted at the ferry and taken to police headquarters for questioning, and the Danish and Swedish police coordinate their zeal. In April, on the same day as a raid on Philipson's house in Copenhagen, Reich's room is searched without a warrant. Nothing is found and no charge is ever raised, but the residence permit dies of it. The Sound closes; they must vanish for a summer.
suggested_refs: Swedish police surveillance files on Wilhelm Reich, Malmö 1934
sources: David Boadella, Wilhelm Reich: The Evolution of His Work (1973), p. 111
Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983)

stops.name: Sletten, the incognito summer
stops.campa: They spend the early summer illegally in Denmark, in the fishing village of Sletten on the Øresund coast, Reich under a false name and Elsa keeping the small house of the vanished. The sea, the boats, the herring-smoke: the two most watched bodies in Scandinavia rest by lying still. In hiding the work goes forward: the vegetative currents, the breath, the musculature of fear, argued out nightly between a doctor with a theory and a dancer with the thing itself.
suggested_refs: The fishing village of Sletten on the Øresund coast, north of Humlebæk
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 200
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: The camp by the lake, honeysuckle and free bodies
stops.campa: In August they drive south across Europe, camping, with Reich's daughters, an idyll the canon preserves in Eva's memory: dancing with Elsa, the smell of honeysuckle all around them, free bodies exercising, bathing in the lakes, Reich tender with Elsa as Eva had rarely seen him with her own mother. By the water near Lucerne the caravan halts. For one summer the family that could not exist, exists: assembled from exiles, and held together by a dancer.
suggested_refs: Eva Reich's recollections of the 1934 camping journey, in Sharaf's Fury on Earth
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 200
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Lucerne, the congress casts him out
stops.campa: At the Thirteenth International Psychoanalytic Congress in Lucerne the guild completes what the states began: Reich is maneuvered out of the International Psychoanalytic Association, hears his case judged in rooms he is not admitted to, and delivers his scheduled lecture as an outcast. Elsa watches the man she crossed borders for come back from the halls a saddened man. Church and Party have both cast him out now; what remains to him is the body, and the woman who knows how it speaks.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the 13th IPA Congress, Lucerne, August 1934
sources: David Boadella, Wilhelm Reich: The Evolution of His Work (1973), p. 114
Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983)

stops.name: Oslo, Drammensveien 110h, the new beginning
stops.campa: By November they are living together at Drammensveien 110h in Oslo, called north by the psychologist Harald Schjelderup to the last radical capital of Europe. Reich will write it later like scripture: Drammensvejen, the new beginning. Here vegetotherapy is built in daily sessions and nightly arguments, and the canon names the era the golden age of body psychotherapy: Reich with the character-analytic theory, Elsa with the somatic art, Raknes and Hoel and the Norwegians gathered round. The city knows her as his second wife, unwed and unashamed.
suggested_refs: The house at Drammensveien 110h, Oslo, where Reich and Lindenberg lived
sources: Wilhelm Reich, Beyond Psychology: Letters & Journals 1934-1939 (1994), p. 230
Ilse Ollendorf Reich, Wilhelm Reich: A Personal Biography (1969), p. 27
https://norgeguide.com/en/oslo/landemerker-og-historiske-steder/wilhelm-reichs-house/

stops.name: Berlin, the child not born
stops.campa: In the new year Elsa is carrying Reich's child, and she is overjoyed; then his doubts set in, the work too unsettled, the future too provisional, and to her great sorrow he insists. She travels to Berlin, where Edith Jacobson of the resistance helps arrange the illegal operation, and in a city ruled by the enemy the child of the dancer and the doctor is not born. Reich writes to her in Berlin that he loves her deeply and wants children with her. The canon lets the wound stand, unhealed and unexplained.
suggested_refs: Reich's letters to Elsa in Berlin, February-March 1935, in Beyond Psychology
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), pp. 245-246
Wilhelm Reich, Beyond Psychology (1994), pp. 23-36
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Oslo, the return in March
stops.campa: In March she returns to Oslo and to work, and the account settles into a rare word for this life: happy. The three years from the fall of 1934 are, the chronicle says, among the happiest of Reich's life, and Elsa is the reason. He supports her independence in principle and mostly in practice; she builds a career of her own beside his, not inside it. In the evenings the household above the fjord fills with seminars, dancers, analysts and refugees. The north is kind for a season.
suggested_refs: The full-page photograph 'Meine Elsa', 1939, in Beyond Psychology
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 245
Wilhelm Reich, Beyond Psychology (1994)

stops.name: Oslo, the workers' stage
stops.campa: The workers' stage takes her: Elsa is engaged with the Arbeiderteatret, choreographing for the red revues at the Arbeidersamfundet: agitprop made flesh, the Berlin street-theatre nights reborn in Norwegian. From 1935 to 1939 she works the workers' theatre while teaching dancers on her own account. The exiled corps-dancer of the Städtische Oper now sets miners' sons and shop-girls moving in formation, and the movement choir of Laban's doctrine discovers what it was always for.
suggested_refs: The Oslo Arbeidersamfundet, house of the workers' revues
sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa_Lindenberg
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich
Ilse Ollendorf Reich, Wilhelm Reich: A Personal Biography (1969), p. 27

stops.name: Oslo, the seminars: ballet changed into Reichian movement
stops.campa: In her Oslo studio Elsa teaches movement that is no longer exactly dance: ballet changed, her students say, into Reichian ways of moving: breath, pulse, the armor found and melted in the muscle. Young Gerda Geddes, in analysis with Raknes, takes lesson after lesson and stands, she will say, at the front of an avant-garde. This is the canon's cradle of dance-movement therapy: a dancer with Gindler's ear and Laban's geometry, applying the psychoanalyst's map of resistance to bodies in motion.
suggested_refs: Gerda Geddes's taped recollections of Elsa Lindenberg's seminars, in Dancer in the Light
sources: Frank Woods, Dancer in the Light: The Life of Gerda 'Pitt' Geddes (2008), p. 70
Michael Heller, The Golden Age of Body Psychotherapy in Oslo II, J. of Body, Movement & Dance in Psychotherapy 2:2 (2007)

stops.name: Dartington Hall, the summer school
stops.campa: In the summer Elsa is invited to Dartington Hall in Devon, the liveliest cultural commune in Europe, to teach at the summer school where the Jooss-Leeder school, Laban's lineage in English exile, keeps the German dance alive. Poets, potters, weavers, dancers; and Reich arriving from his European rounds to join her among them. At Dartington also waits Gerd Bergersen, the young Norwegian weaver, of whom the chronicle will have more to say. The English summer folds the whole diaspora of the body into one green estate.
suggested_refs: Dartington Hall, Totnes, Devon, courtyard and gardens of the 1930s summer schools
sources: Colin Wilson, The Quest for Wilhelm Reich (1981), pp. 200-201
Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 255
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Oslo, the Sexpol rebuke
stops.campa: The first crack is doctrinal. Elsa speaks her mind about the Sexpol circle: neurotics, she says, rubbish, bourgeois. Reich answers in a letter with the full weight of the founder's office: as founder of the Sexpol movement he must protest. After this she stays away from the meetings. In his journal he mourns and rages in the same week: how he loved Elsa, how her illness destroys everything, how he wants a child by her. The bions are breeding in his laboratory, and the marriage of theory and dance is straining.
suggested_refs: Reich's journal entries of November 1936, in Beyond Psychology
sources: Wilhelm Reich, Beyond Psychology (1994), pp. 72-82
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Oslo, the newspaper war begins
stops.campa: From the autumn of 1937 the Oslo press opens its campaign against Reich: month after month of mockery and denunciation, the mill of Norwegian respectability grinding the foreign doctor and his life-substance. Elsa watches the man change under it. He ceases, old friends say, to be so good a therapist; he begins to crush people; and his suspicion turns homeward. Her career, her colleagues, her separate world, all begin to look to him like the face of the outside that is attacking him.
suggested_refs: The Oslo newspaper campaign against Reich, 1937-38, press cuttings
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), pp. 253-254
Ilse Ollendorf Reich, Wilhelm Reich: A Personal Biography (1969), p. 45

stops.name: Oslo, the blackened eye and the hardest no
stops.campa: The jealousy breaks into the open: Reich blacks the eye of a musician colleague of Elsa's, and Elsa refuses to go home with him, taking refuge with a friend. He follows, accuses, and somehow they reconcile, but the relationship is scarred and she knows it. Soon after, he asks her whether she will emigrate to America with him. She answers no. She must get back to herself, protect her independence against his demands, and decide in freedom whether she wants him at all.
stops.quote: It was the hardest 'no' I ever had to say.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Lindenberg to Myron Sharaf, interview, Oslo 1977; Fury on Earth, p. 254
suggested_refs: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth: A Biography of Wilhelm Reich (1983)
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), pp. 254-255
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Oslo, a place of her own
stops.campa: Reich has decided for America; in the spring Elsa separates and finds a place of her own in Oslo. There is no settlement, Reich holds that a woman able to earn has no right to alimony, and she asks for none. He writes to her in April and they meet once more, two sovereignties negotiating a border. The door is not closed: he may send for her, she may follow. But the household on Drammensveien is ended, and each keeps what each brought: he the theory, she the dance.
suggested_refs: Reich's letter to Elsa of 18 April 1939, in Beyond Psychology
sources: Ilse Ollendorf Reich, Wilhelm Reich: A Personal Biography (1969), pp. 45-46
Wilhelm Reich, Beyond Psychology (1994)

stops.name: Drammensveien, the last evening
stops.campa: While visa delays hold Reich in Oslo through the summer, there is a last evening together. Tonight Elsa was with me, he writes in his journal; we both knew that the separation is both necessary and tragic. There is a part of me, he writes, that she understood better than anyone else; her morals are those of a beautiful wild animal that acts in accordance with its nature. It is the truest portrait anyone ever makes of her, and it is written in farewell.
suggested_refs: Reich's journal entry of 4 August 1939, in Beyond Psychology
sources: Wilhelm Reich, Beyond Psychology (1994), p. 228

stops.name: Oslo harbor, the ship she does not board
stops.campa: The ship sails for New York with Reich aboard and Elsa on the quay of her own decision. From the sea he writes that he cried a good deal on the trip, that he misses her, that he wants her to follow. Within weeks the war closes the ocean; within months he has met Ilse Ollendorf, whose body reminds him of Elsa's. The letters go on for years: tender, chiding, then business-like, then silent. Elsa remains in Oslo with her work, her students, and the hardest no she ever said.
suggested_refs: The SS Stavangerfjord, last peacetime crossing from Oslo to New York, August 1939
sources: Wilhelm Reich, Beyond Psychology (1994), pp. 229-230
Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 274

stops.name: Oslo, the ninth of April
stops.campa: German soldiers march down Karl Johans gate; Norway is occupied in a morning. For Elsa the trap of Berlin has crossed the sea and sprung again: a German Communist, expelled from a state opera for damaging the state, companion of the Reich's most scandalous exile, standing in an occupied capital under her own true name. She loses her theatre work. The golden age of the Oslo body is over, and the age of hiding begins.
suggested_refs: Photographs of German troops on Karl Johans gate, Oslo, 9 April 1940
sources: Ilse Ollendorf Reich, Wilhelm Reich: A Personal Biography (1969), pp. 45-46
Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 274

stops.name: Oslo, underground, the marriage of convenience
stops.campa: The Gestapo begins asking after her. To blunt the investigations Elsa contracts a marriage of convenience with a Norwegian, taking a citizen's name over her endangered one: a wedding as camouflage, a ring as forged papers. She goes underground in the city she taught to move, penniless through the war winters; once she overcomes her pride and writes to Reich in America for help, and he sends twenty-five dollars. The canon records the sum without comment.
suggested_refs: Ida Korsvold's account of the war years, in Karina & Kant, Hitler's Dancers
sources: Lilian Karina & Marion Kant, Hitler's Dancers (2003)
Ilse Ollendorf Reich, Wilhelm Reich: A Personal Biography (1969), pp. 45-46

stops.name: The border forests, flight into Sweden
stops.campa: By 1944 her name stands on the lists of the wanted, an enemy of the German state hunted in an occupied land, and Elsa goes over the border the way the Resistance goes: into the frontier forests, through the snow, into Sweden. The dancer's body, trained for forty years to be exactly itself, carries her across. Behind her Oslo keeps her students, her sham marriage and her furniture; ahead lie neutral ground and the long wait.
suggested_refs: The wartime refugee routes over the Norwegian-Swedish border in Østfold
sources: Lilian Karina & Marion Kant, Hitler's Dancers (2003)
https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa_Lindenberg

stops.name: Sweden, hidden until the end
stops.campa: In Sweden she hides until the end of the war, one refugee among the thousands the Norwegian night has pushed over the frontier. Stateless in effect, wed in name only, twice exiled: the German who fled Germany, now the German fled out of Norway. In borrowed rooms she waits out the last winter of the Reich that expelled her from her stage eleven years before, and she outlives it, as the body outlives the doctrine that condemned it.
suggested_refs: Records of Norwegian wartime refugees in Sweden, 1943-45
sources: Lilian Karina & Marion Kant, Hitler's Dancers (2003)
Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 274

stops.name: Oslo, the bitter return
stops.campa: Norway is free and Elsa returns to Oslo: into a liberation with no place for her. She is German, and the freed country for a time punishes the language itself: she is persecuted as an enemy national, she who stood on the wanted lists of the Gestapo. The injustice is exact and total, and the canon does not soften it. In the summer of 1945 the woman who said no to America stands in Oslo owning nothing but the method in her body.
suggested_refs: Liberation photographs, Oslo, May-June 1945
sources: Lilian Karina & Marion Kant, Hitler's Dancers (2003)
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

segments.name: The Method and the Long Evening

stops.name: Oslo, the school of movement, the therapy of the dance
stops.campa: She begins again, teaching. For years after the war Elsa teaches a form of dance therapy shaped by Reich's psychiatric concepts, the work she made beside him in the golden years, now hers alone: tension and release, breath and expression, the armor read in the moving body. In Norway the lineage she planted flows into the country's own school of the body: Bülow-Hansen, Braatøy, the psychomotor tradition. A form of her dance-movement work is practiced there still. The canon calls her a founding mother of the discipline.
suggested_refs: The Norwegian psychomotor physiotherapy tradition, heir of the Oslo golden age
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), p. 275
Michael Heller, The Golden Age of Body Psychotherapy in Oslo I-II (2007)
Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich

stops.name: Oslo, rehabilitated, the state's pension
stops.campa: The state makes its amends: Elsa Lindenberg is rehabilitated by the Norwegian government and awarded a state pension. The file that began with a Berlin warrant in 1933, enemy of the German state, then enemy German, closes at last with a Norwegian apology and a monthly sum. She accepts it as she accepted the scholarship at thirteen: as owed to the body that earned it. Oslo is now, finally and officially, her city, and will be to the end.
suggested_refs: Ida Korsvold's account of the rehabilitation, in Karina & Kant, Hitler's Dancers
sources: Lilian Karina & Marion Kant, Hitler's Dancers (2003)
https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsa_Lindenberg

stops.name: Berlin, Gindler again
stops.campa: She returns to Berlin, the wound inspected once more, to study again with Elsa Gindler, her teacher before the war and after it, who has survived the destruction of her studio and teaches on amid the rubble-city. The quiet work resumes as if twenty years of catastrophe were an interruption between two breaths. Lindenberg carries the Gindler method back north and becomes, in Oslo, its much-respected teacher: guardian of a doctrine that was never written down.
suggested_refs: Elsa Gindler's postwar Berlin courses, remembered by her students

stops.name: Oslo, the chair and the swan
stops.campa: A car accident has broken her hip and ended her dancing; Elsa leads her Oslo classes from a chair, grey-haired and heavy now, scolding her students, physiotherapists who come to her secretly, against their teacher's moral disapproval of the unwed wife, for moving without feeling. One day, failing to explain in words, she rises from the chair and dances. The grey duckling, Berit Bunkan will remember, became a beautiful swan, soft, fantastic and elegant, and the students wept. Then she sits back down. The lesson is complete.
suggested_refs: Berit Heir Bunkan's memoir of Elsa Lindenberg's classes, addendum to Courtenay Young's article
sources: Berit Heir Bunkan, addendum to Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich (2010)

stops.name: Oslo, the small flat, Willy's picture
stops.campa: In a small Oslo flat, a picture of Wilhelm Reich on the wall beside her chair, Elsa receives visitors as Willy's second wife and rules the Scandinavian body-work as its dowager. When Miriam Goldberg comes from Israel to teach, Elsa summons her and asks, terribly, how she dares bring Charlotte Selver's method into her domain in short courses that can do damage. The room is electric; the visitors stand. The guardianship is absolute: what Gindler never wrote down, Lindenberg will not see cheapened.
suggested_refs: Berit Heir Bunkan's account of the meeting with Miriam Goldberg
sources: Berit Heir Bunkan, addendum to Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich (2010)

stops.name: Oslo, Sharaf's visit
stops.campa: Myron Sharaf, writing the great biography of Reich, comes to Oslo and finds her at seventy strikingly attractive and vivacious. She speaks of Willy with tenderness, passion, humor and criticism at once: the jealous rages, the affairs, the abrupt ending after the passionate letters of 1939, all folded into a deep, genuine and unsentimental love. After Reich, she tells him, there was never another serious man; she was in her early thirties when they parted. Her testimony becomes a wellspring of the canon itself: Fury on Earth speaks with her voice.
suggested_refs: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), the chapters drawn from the 1977 Oslo interviews
sources: Myron Sharaf, Fury on Earth (1983), pp. 245, 254, 274-275

stops.name: Lovisenberg Hospital, the last interview
stops.campa: In the early summer of 1990, old and ill in Lovisenberg Hospital, Elsa gives her last interview, to the Swedish journalist Anna Britta Staal with Berit Bunkan at the bedside. Pale in the bed, she begins to speak of Willy and her eyes sparkle, her face turns lively and rosy; she remembers the free sexuality of the golden household, where everything was natural. And she leaves the record one final correction: her last word on the hardest no ever said.
stops.quote: People think it was because of disagreement about the therapy that I did not go with Willy to USA, but that was not the reason.
stops.quote_source: Last interview, Lovisenberg Hospital, Oslo, summer 1990; recorded by Berit Heir Bunkan
suggested_refs: Lovisenberg Diakonale Sykehus, Oslo
sources: Berit Heir Bunkan, addendum to Courtenay Young, On Elsa Lindenberg and Reich (2010)

stops.name: Oslo, the death of the dancer
stops.campa: On the sixth of November 1990 Elsa Lindenberg dies in Oslo, eighty-four years old, fifty-one years after the quay. Her papers pass to her friend Ida Korsvold, who lets no one see them: the archive keeps its silence like Gindler's unwritten method, and the biographers must make do with everyone else's letters. What cannot be sealed is the inheritance: body psychotherapy and dance-movement therapy, the two children of the union of the doctor and the dancer, both alive, both still moving.
